newsitem.title: USA: U.S. revives sidetracked ergonomic standard effort.
newsitem.headline: U.S. revives sidetracked ergonomic standard effort.

text.p: The Clinton administration will resume its drive to develop ergonomic standards aimed at preventing costly repetitive stress injuries (RSI) in the workplace, Labor Secretary Robert Reich said Tuesday.

The effort, which had been blocked by Congress, will resume with an open solicitation for information, he said. It is aimed at tackling the fastest growing and costliest of workplace injuries, accounting for one-third of the $60 billion in annual workers' compensations costs.
"There's a great deal of evidence, mounting evidence, that a problem exists," said Reich, who has announced that he will leave the administration by next month.
"We are going to continue exploring this issue," he told reporters. "We are going to continue doing everything we can to protect workers from these sorts of injuries."

A draft of a proposed ergonomics standard developed by the department's Occupational Safety and Health Administration (OSHA) two years ago was sidetracked when Congress blocked the agency from spending any money to continue the effort during the fiscal year that ended on Sept. 30.
Reich said that the drive to come up with standards aimed at preventing RSI would continue, regardless of who replaces him as labor secretary.
"The administration is 100 percent behind moving foward," he said. "The president is committed to it. My successor, working for the president, is also committed to it."

In the new effort, however, the administration said it will seek consensus around specific types of RSI problems by involving experts from labor, academia and business, which criticized the previous draft as a "one-size-fits-all" solution to a complex problem.
OSHA Administrator Joseph Dear said the agency first will determine where the problems are most severe and the solutions are the most well-known.

"The attempt will be to build an understanding around that and develop a standard from that based on that understanding," he said. "It's too soon to say what the standard will look like or when it would be ready for proposal to the public."
RSI, a painful and potentially debilitating injury, is caused by repetitive motion, usually of hands or arms.

The three most common causes of RSI cited by OSHA are speeding up production lines, especially in the poultry industry, intensive keyboard work in a huge number of office workplaces, and repetitive heavy lifting.
RSI accounts for one out of every four lost-time injuries and claims for it are twice as costly as the average workers' compensation claim.

Last week, a federal jury in Brooklyn, N.Y., awarded nearly $6 million to three women for arm, wrist and hand injuries from using keyboards made by Digital Equipment Corp. The company has said it would appeal.
Reich, who blamed Washington-based business groups for halting the department's earlier RSI effort, said business has an economic interest in preventing these injuries.
An RSI standard would set up enforceable workplace systems and practices, unlike guidelines that now exist in the meatpacking industry, which lack teeth.

OSHA has launched some 400 ergonomic enforcement cases against employers in the past 10 years, citing violations of their "general duty" to maintain safe workplaces. Reich called that tactic "an inefficient way of dealing with the problem."
